The biggest order, the smallest cash balance (FIN-03) is a Micro Cases classroom video on whether a profitable order is still fundable when the cash arrives later than the bills.

You run a fictional Hong Kong promotional-gift packing workshop. A new customer offers your biggest order yet: HK$120,000. You have spare capacity, so it will not displace other work. The initial quote requires full payment today, before materials are bought. You have HK$40,000 in available cash and must keep at least HK$20,000 as a safety buffer. Other business receipts and payments are separately funded. No costs have yet been committed, and declining the order leaves your HK$40,000 unchanged. Under the initial quote, the customer pays HK$120,000 today, you then buy materials for this order for HK$50,000, and on day 7 you pay HK$30,000 for additional packing staff and deliver. There are no other incremental costs in this simplified case. Ignore taxes, interest and default risk for the first vote. Would you accept the order on these terms? Calculate what it adds to earnings and the lowest cash balance after acceptance.

The teaching format is pause, vote, and reveal. Pause at each decision, vote, compare your reasons, then continue for the debrief. A later fact changes what you know about when the customer pays, and you vote again.

The workshop, the customer, the order, the amounts, the timing and the buffer are invented teaching assumptions, not survey observations, and not a news report about any real company.

The invoice is not the exposure (FIN-04) is a Micro Cases classroom video on checking yen receipts and payments before deciding how much currency uncertainty to carry.

Fictional classroom situation. You own a Hong Kong stationery wholesaler. A Japanese supplier must receive JPY1,000,000 in 30 days. Your first budget assumes you will buy all those yen using Hong Kong dollars on the payment date. The accountant shows two possible exchange-rate scenarios, which are invented comparison rates, not current quotes or forecasts: at HK$0.050 per yen, buying JPY1,000,000 costs HK$50,000; at HK$0.055 per yen, it costs HK$55,000. The higher rate would require HK$5,000 more if you bought the entire invoice amount. No probabilities are supplied. Ignore conversion fees in the arithmetic. You want to decide how much supplier-payment uncertainty to carry. There is time to inspect all yen receipts and payments before arranging anything. No financial product has been priced or purchased. Would you seek budget certainty for the full invoice, leave the amount uncertain, or check other yen cash flows first? What information could change your answer?

The teaching format is pause, vote, and reveal. Pause at each decision, vote, compare your reasons, then continue for the debrief. A later fact changes what you know about other yen cash flows, and you vote again.

The wholesaler, the invoices, the dates and the exchange rates are invented teaching assumptions, not a news report about any real company.

A larger limit. The same gap? (FIN-05) is a Micro Cases classroom video on whether raising an insurance limit is the same as better protection.

Fictional classroom situation. A Hong Kong craft-workshop studio reviews its weather protection before the next storm season. The owner remembers losing business when customers could not attend. Its current interruption policy pays verified covered interruption loss only following insured physical damage at its own premises, up to HK$100,000. For this exercise there are no non-damage, access-denial, utility or supplier extensions. Ignore deductibles and waiting periods solely to isolate the issue. For an additional HK$2,000 annual premium, the studio can increase that limit to HK$200,000. Nothing else changes. The owner says: “Twice the protection should make us ready.” Would you approve the higher limit now, keep the current limit, or investigate first? What must you know before calling it twice the protection?

The teaching format is pause, vote, and reveal. Pause at each decision, vote, compare your reasons, then continue for the debrief. A later fact changes what you know about the planning scenario, and you vote again.

The studio, the quotations and the simplified policy terms are invented teaching assumptions, not a real insurance recommendation, and not a news report about any real company.

Smaller payments. Cheaper loan? (FIN-06) is a Micro Cases classroom video on whether smaller monthly payments mean a cheaper loan.

Fictional classroom situation. A Hong Kong appliance-repair workshop needs HK$100,000 for replacement equipment. Two lenders have sent financing quotes. Each would advance exactly HK$100,000. Quote A asks for HK$4,500 a month; Quote B asks for HK$2,500 a month. The owner favours B: “We keep HK$2,000 more each month for wages and parts. That must be the cheaper loan.” The bookkeeper has the monthly figures but has not yet checked the full payment schedules. Your job is to make a provisional recommendation, not approve an incomplete contract. The business values a cash buffer, but its future monthly cash flows have not been supplied. No return on retained cash is assumed. Would you provisionally favour B for its smaller payments? What must you check before calling it cheaper or deciding the workshop can afford either loan?

The teaching format is pause, vote, and reveal. Pause at each decision, vote, compare your reasons, then continue for the debrief. A later fact changes what you know about the full payment schedules, and you vote again.

The workshop and the loan quotes are invented teaching assumptions, not offers under any support programme, and not a news report about any real company.

A discount for paying sooner. Sooner than what? (FIN-07) is a Micro Cases classroom video on what “paying sooner” is being compared with when a settlement discount is offered.

Fictional classroom situation. An exhibition-display supplier has ten existing, undisputed invoices of HK$100,000 each. All were issued on day 0 and are formally due on day 60. It is considering a one-off 2% discount for payment on day 10. If offered, all ten customers would pay HK$98,000 on day 10; this is an explicit classroom assumption. The sales manager assumes that, without the offer, all ten would pay on day 60. Under that assumed baseline, each accelerated invoice avoids HK$3,000 of all-in bridging-finance cost between days 10 and 60, the discount is HK$2,000 per invoice or HK$20,000 for all ten, the assumed financing cost avoided is HK$30,000, and the net benefit under that baseline is HK$10,000. The HK$3,000 is a supplied, fully avoidable marginal cost, not an interest rate or bank quote. The offer has not been made. On the manager’s assumed payment baseline, would you provisionally approve the blanket discount? Name one concrete piece of payment-behaviour evidence that would reverse your recommendation.

The teaching format is pause, vote, and reveal. Pause at each decision, vote, compare your reasons, then continue for the debrief. A later fact changes what you know about when customers would pay without the offer, and you vote again.

The invoices, dates, take-up and costs are invented teaching assumptions, not a news report about any real company.

虚构的课堂情境。一家展览展示供应商有十张既有、没有争议的发票，每张100,000港元。全部在第0天开出，正式到期日是第60天。它在考虑一次性给2%的折扣，条件是第10天付款。如果提出，十个客户都会在第10天付98,000港元；这是课堂上写明的假设。销售经理假定：不提这个折扣，十个客户都会在第60天付款。在这个假定基准下，每张被提前的发票可以避开第10天到第60天之间3,000港元的全部过渡融资成本；每张折扣2,000港元，十个客户合计20,000港元；假定避开的融资成本是30,000港元；该基准下的净好处是10,000港元。这3,000港元是题目给定、可以完全避开的边际成本，不是利率，也不是银行报价。折扣还没有提出。按经理假定的付款基准，你会暂时批准这个一揽子折扣吗？说出一项具体的付款行为证据，它会让你反过来。

QNdl2tdO-lw.description:
Back sooner. Worth more? (FIN-08) is a Micro Cases classroom video on whether a shorter payback means a more valuable investment.

Fictional classroom situation. A Hong Kong training studio has one spare room and two alternative fit-out plans. A supports an established short-course format with stronger early demand. B supports a programme expected to build over time. Either costs HK$100,000 today and runs for the same four-year remaining lease. Only one can occupy the room. Doing neither is also possible. Cash and operating reserves are sufficient for either plan. The owner’s summary says A pays back at the end of year 2, B at the end of year 3. “Why wait an extra year?” she asks. The full four-year estimates have not yet been compared. Plan A’s year-1 and year-2 net receipts are HK$60,000 and HK$40,000; Plan B’s are HK$20,000 and HK$40,000. Net receipts mean incremental cash after all relevant operating costs, maintenance, working-capital movements and tax, not sales or accounting profit. Which plan would you provisionally favour? Is the shorter payback enough to commit, and what is missing from this comparison?

The teaching format is pause, vote, and reveal. Pause at each decision, vote, compare your reasons, then continue for the debrief. A later fact changes what you know about the later years, and you vote again.

The studio, the fit-outs, the cash flows and the later review are invented teaching assumptions, not a news report about any real company or project.

oE09NSa8aoA.description:
One bank. Two kinds of safety. (FIN-09) is a Micro Cases classroom video on two kinds of safety for a bank deposit: how much is protected, and whether the money can be used when a payment is due.

On 1 October 2024, Hong Kong raised its Deposit Protection Scheme limit to HK$800,000 per depositor per member bank. That is not a separate allowance for each account or a promise of immediate spending access. Fictional classroom situation. Harbour Print Limited is deciding where to keep HK$1.2 million of its own operating reserve. It can keep everything at Bank A or divide it equally between Bank A and Bank B. The company is an eligible depositor. These are conventional on-demand Hong Kong-dollar deposits at Hong Kong offices of two confirmed, separate Deposit Protection Scheme member banks. Keeping the reserve together offers more illustrated interest and less administration: a fictional 3% at Bank A illustrates HK$36,000 a year, with HK$800,000 of the starting principal within the protection ceiling. Dividing it equally places HK$600,000 at each bank, at fictional rates of 3% and 2.8%, illustrating HK$34,800 of interest, plus HK$1,800 of extra administration cost, so the comparison cost is HK$3,000 a year; the starting principal then sits within the ceilings across both banks. Accrued interest counts within the protection limit, not on top of it. The task is to choose a policy, not to open accounts or move real money. Keep the reserve together or divide it? What would justify the extra HK$3,000 annual comparison cost, and what evidence could reverse your choice?

The teaching format is pause, vote, and reveal. Pause at each decision, vote, compare your reasons, then continue for the debrief. A later fact changes what you know about payment access, and you vote again.

The company, the banks, the rates and the costs are invented teaching assumptions, not a news report about any real bank, and no named bank is alleged to be unsafe.

Twenty per cent. Only once? (FIN-10) is a Micro Cases classroom video on whether giving up 20% of a company happens only once in an expansion.

Fictional classroom situation. LightBench, a Hong Kong product-photography studio, is considering an expansion. Current owners collectively hold 100%. Existing services, wages, rent and required reserves remain funded and viable without expanding; the owners can decline both offers. Phase 1 needs HK$400,000 for a complete tabletop-product service that is useful on its own. Optional Phase 2 adds a larger-object service for another HK$600,000. Two illustrative new-share offers are available before commitment. Funds enter the company, not the owners’ pockets. No profit or future company-value forecast is supplied. Offer A funds the first phase only, raising HK$400,000 for 20% of the company immediately after issue, leaving original owners with 80%. Offer B funds both phases, raising HK$1,000,000 for 30%, leaving original owners with 70%. A needs a later financing decision if Phase 2 is chosen. B permits pausing Phase 2 and keeping unused funds in the company, but pausing spending does not reverse shares already issued. Which route would you provisionally prefer, and why? Does 20% now establish that A preserves more ownership through the whole expansion? Name future-funding evidence that could change your answer.

The teaching format is pause, vote, and reveal. Pause at each decision, vote, compare your reasons, then continue for the debrief. A later fact changes what you know about later financing, and you vote again.

The studio, the offers and the budgets are invented teaching assumptions, not a news report about any real company.
